bull_thesis: The bull case is that a genuinely sale-able franchise finally transacts, and it transacts high enough to leave real money for common shareholders. The ingredients are there. AlTi Global is an independent global wealth manager with $90.1 billion of assets under advisement and $48.7 billion under management, serving more than 830 ultra-wealthy families at an average relationship of about $60 million, with 96% client retention since 2021. That is an authentic, sticky franchise. The operating trajectory is improving, not decaying: first-quarter 2026 revenue was $73 million, up 28%, with adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) of $14.9 million, up 21%, and a margin of 20% against 13% the prior quarter. Management targets $20 million of recurring annual gross savings by the end of 2026. Since December 9, 2025 the board has run a formal review with J.P. Morgan as banker and Wachtell, Lipton as counsel, and the catalyst density is unusual: three separate insiders have filed activist Schedule 13D notices. Allianz holds about 26% of the Class A stock, having bought common at $5.69 with warrants struck at $7.40; Constellation Wealth Capital holds $150 million of Series C preferred plus common with warrants at the same $7.40; and co-founder Michael Tiedemann, ousted as chief executive on March 30, 2026, holds 9.8% and has disclosed he is exploring a take-private. Those insider marks sit well above today's $3.58. For the bull case to work, three things must hold: a bidder must bridge a valuation gap that press reporting puts at more than $600 million; the price must clear the $352 million preferred stack with enough left over for the common; and it must happen before the 9.75% compounding dividend grows that stack much further. If a strategic buyer pays a full multiple for scarce ultra-wealthy distribution rather than a sponsor's cash-flow multiple, the common can reach the mid-$4s.
bear_thesis: The bear case is not that the sale fails. It is that the arithmetic says the sale cannot succeed at a price that helps common shareholders, and that waiting costs money. Start with the capital structure, because it is the whole story. At the March 31, 2026 balance sheet, the common is worth about $529 million at $3.58, but sitting ahead of it is $352.2 million of preferred stock, plus $37.5 million of net debt. That implies an enterprise value near $919 million. Annualize the best quarter the company has printed and adjusted EBITDA is about $60 million; be generous and credit the full $20 million cost programme. The enterprise is therefore trading at roughly 15 times EBITDA. Private-equity buyers underwrite wealth managers at 9 to 13 times. At 12 to 13 times on $58 to $60 million, the whole enterprise is worth $700 to $780 million; subtract net debt and the preferred, and the common is left with roughly $2.10 to $2.65 a share. That is the reported $600 million gap, and it is not a haggle to be split. Buyers say so directly: press reporting quotes a mathematical disparity between what a sponsor would pay on a reasonable multiple of AlTi's cash flow and its current market cap and enterprise value — meaning the bidders think the stock is already too expensive. That explains every fact on the tape: why Corient and other consolidators were rebuffed, why eleven months with J.P. Morgan (retained August 2025) have produced nothing, and why interim chief executive Nancy Curtin says no proposal captures the long-term value. There is no floor beneath this. Tangible common equity is roughly negative $550 million once $815.9 million of goodwill and intangibles is removed. The company has lost money on a reported basis every year since listing: $165.6 million in 2023, $103.0 million in 2024, $119.7 million in 2025. Cash is $39.7 million. Nothing contractual, tangible or earnings-based backstops the quote. Worse, time is short the common: the Series A and Series C preferred each compound at 9.75%, costing roughly $34 million a year all-in, and part of that is settled in newly issued stock at depressed prices — Allianz received 1,272,328 Class A shares on July 2, 2026. Every quarter of delay grows the claim ahead of the common and the share count beneath it. Earnings quality is also thinner than the headline: $21 million of the $73 million quarter was lumpy investment distributions, up 75% year over year, against $52 million of recurring fees. The core franchise posted net client outflows of $0.2 billion in the first quarter of 2026. What confirms the bear: the review lapses or goes quiet, or a deal prints at a price that barely serves the common after the preferred is paid.
sop_bull: The event-win case is about $4.40 per share. Assume a strategic acquirer, not a sponsor, pays up for scarce ultra-wealthy distribution: 16 times a post-savings adjusted EBITDA of $65 million gives an enterprise value of roughly $1,040 million. Subtract $37.5 million of net debt to get $1,002 million, then subtract the $352 million preferred claim, leaving about $650 million for roughly 148.5 million economic shares (Class A plus the Class B units of the up-C partnership structure) — about $4.40. A cross-check on assets under management gives a similar answer: registered-investment-adviser deals price around 2 to 3 percent of assets under management, and 2.5 percent of $48.7 billion is about $1.2 billion of enterprise value, which after the preferred and net debt leaves roughly $5.45 a share at the top end. Note what the base of this case requires: a full 16 times, above the 9 to 13 times sponsors actually pay, and a buyer willing to fund the preferred in full. The insider reference marks — Allianz's $5.69 common basis and the $7.40 warrant strike — are cost bases, not valuations, and the arithmetic does not reach them.
sop_bear: The adverse case is about $2.30 per share, and it is a market marker rather than a verified floor — which is the finding. If the review lapses, distributions normalize and adjusted EBITDA settles near $52 million, a sponsor multiple of 10 times gives a $520 million enterprise value; less $37.5 million of net debt and the $352 million preferred leaves roughly $130 million, or about $0.88 a share. The market is unlikely to mark it there quickly, so the practical adverse case is a break of the $2.75 fifty-two-week low toward roughly $2.30. Critically, nothing halts a further slide: tangible common equity is about negative $550 million, the company has never posted a reported profit, cash is $39.7 million, and the common is a residual claim behind a preferred stack that compounds at 9.75% and pays part of itself in new shares.
sop_breakdown: Probability-weighted across the two live outcomes, because the common's value hinges entirely on whether a sale clears the preferred stack. The underlying enterprise is worth about $750 million on a base case of 12.5 times a normalized $58 to $60 million of adjusted EBITDA — that is the wealth-management franchise: $90.1 billion of assets under advisement, $48.7 billion under management, more than 830 ultra-wealthy relationships, 96% retention, plus the lumpier investment distributions. From that enterprise value, subtract $37.5 million of net debt and the $352.2 million accreted preferred claim held by Allianz and Constellation, leaving about $360 million for roughly 148.5 million economic shares, or about $2.40 a share on fundamentals alone. Layering the event on top: a strategic take-out near $4.40 at roughly 25% odds, blended with a no-deal drift toward $2.50 at roughly 75% odds, gives about $2.85. Either route lands below the live price of $3.58. The preferred is the entire bridge between a respectable business and a poor stock: it takes the first $352 million of any sale, and it compounds at 9.75% — about $34 million a year all-in, or roughly $0.23 a share annually — with part of it settled in newly issued common.
risk_reward: Negative asymmetry — roughly 0.65 to 1. Upside to a full strategic take-out at $4.40 is about +23% from $3.58; downside to a break of the fifty-two-week low at $2.30 is about -35%. The ratio is worse than one-to-one before weighting, and the undated, deadlocked no-deal path is the likelier of the two. This is the inverse of a defined-risk special situation: the reward is capped by the preferred stack and the risk is unbounded by any verified floor.
catalyst_summary: An undated, eleven-month-stale sale process that the company has now stepped back from -- on the May 11, 2026 call the interim chief executive said AlTi is "evaluating opportunities that come as opposed to a strategic review process in place at the moment" -- deadlocked on a reported $600 million-plus valuation gap because roughly $352 million of preferred compounding at 9.75% consumes whatever a real wealth-manager multiple would pay. Upside to a generous strategic take-out is about +23% against about -35% to a low retest, with no verified floor and the clock running against the common.
dated_milestone: No binding deal date exists. The December 9, 2025 announcement forming the special committee states there is "no definitive timeline set for the completion of the review process," and eleven months after J.P. Morgan was retained there is still no buyer, no price and no drop-dead date. Two natural forcing windows have now passed without incident: the June 17, 2026 annual meeting was held with a routine slate of seven directors plus auditor ratification -- no proxy contest, no consent solicitation, no resolution of the review -- and on June 25, 2026 the company announced chief financial officer succession effective July 1, framed as "a long-planned internal leadership transition designed to support AlTi's next phase of growth," which is standalone language rather than deal language. The only verified hard dates are supply events that cut against the thesis: the Series A preferred transfer restriction lapses July 31, 2026 and a further 30% of Allianz's common becomes transferable that date under its staged lock-up (full release July 31, 2027), and a Form S-3 resale shelf went effective around July 10, 2026 registering 3,053,263 Class A shares -- about 2.8% of the 110.7 million Class A outstanding -- for holders who took stock in the April 2023 Alvarium acquisition.
forcing_function: There is no scheduled trigger, and that is the verdict. The most load-bearing evidence in this file is what the company itself said on May 11, 2026. Asked by a Raymond James analyst when strategic-review expenses would normalize, interim chief executive Nancy Curtin answered: "Obviously, if any proposal comes to the company, to the Board, the Board will need to evaluate it consistent with its fiduciary responsibilities. So it's hard to be sure that all the costs are behind us. But broadly, we have a very laser-focused really just evaluating opportunities that come as opposed to a strategic review process in place at the moment." Read plainly, the formal sale process is no longer running -- the company has shifted from actively marketing itself to passively receiving whatever arrives. Chief financial officer Mike Harrington corroborated the wind-down on cost grounds: review expenses "should start to diminish back half of the year... contingent on the process being complete." Note the divergence between the prepared remarks ("the committee continues its work") and the unscripted answer twenty minutes later; the script preserves the board's optionality, the Q&A describes the actual state, and advisory fees are the truest instrument for measuring whether a banker is still working. They are being guided down. A re-rating would require a signed, priced take-private that bridges the $600 million-plus gap and clears the $352 million preferred with room to spare -- no such agreement, and no timeline, exists. The alternative trigger would be activist escalation by one of the three Schedule 13D filers: Allianz (most capable, but bound by a standstill through July 31, 2027 -- and a conflicted insider who holds the very instrument that caps everyone else's value, with no disclosed majority-of-the-minority protection), Constellation, or ousted co-founder Michael Tiedemann (9.8%, exploring a take-private, though observers doubt he can raise the capital against a backdrop where J.P. Morgan found no partner in eleven months). The June 17, 2026 annual meeting was the natural forcing window and it passed uncontested. The only dated events on the calendar -- the July 31, 2026 transfer-restriction lapse and the July 10, 2026 resale shelf -- add supply rather than forcing value out. Meanwhile the payment-in-kind preferred dividend acts as a reverse forcing function, compounding the claim ahead of the common at 9.75% and settling part of itself in newly issued stock at depressed prices.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market is not about the business — it is about the capital structure, and we think almost nobody is doing the arithmetic. The prevailing frame treats AlTi as a cheap option on a sale: the stock is down about 64% from its $10 January 2023 listing, three activists are circling, and J.P. Morgan is running a process. The street's first error is anchoring on insider cost bases — Allianz's $5.69 common basis and the $7.40 warrant strike — as if they were valuations. They are the marks of investors who bought before the preferred compounded and before the stock halved. Sunk cost is not fair value. The second and most important error is reading the stalled process as a negotiation that patience will resolve. It is not. The $600 million gap exists because a rational buyer's multiple leaves the common at roughly $2.10 to $2.65 after the preferred is served — below today's $3.58. The bidders are not lowballing; they are correct, and they have said so in terms the market has not absorbed: press reporting quotes a mathematical disparity between what a sponsor would pay on a reasonable multiple of AlTi's cash flow and its current market cap and enterprise value. Read that plainly — the buyers think the stock is already too expensive. When the bidders' complaint is that the tape is above their pay-line, the sale is not a source of upside; it is a source of price discovery downward. The third error is crediting a headline quarter without reading its composition: $21 million of the $73 million was lumpy investment distributions up 75% year over year, and the wealth franchise posted net client outflows of $0.2 billion in the same quarter. Our differentiated view is therefore uncomfortable and bearish: the market is pricing sale optionality as free upside when the sale, at any realistic clearing price, is roughly a wash-to-down outcome for common shareholders. The one thing that could make us wrong is a strategic buyer paying well above sponsor economics for scarce ultra-wealthy distribution — a real possibility, and the reason this is a pass rather than a short — but that is the bull case at 16 times, and it still only gets to about $4.40.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months carry supply and dilution risk with no offsetting scheduled catalyst. First, the payment-in-kind dividend is the slow bleed and it is already running: the preferred stack has accreted from $339.7 million at September 30, 2025 to $345.8 million at December 31, 2025 to $352.2 million at March 31, 2026 — about $6.25 million a quarter on the balance sheet, and roughly $34 million a year in full economic cost at the 9.75% compounding rate, because part of the Series A dividend is settled in newly issued Class A shares rather than added to the preferred balance. On July 2, 2026 Allianz received 1,272,328 Class A shares on that mechanic. The claim ahead of the common grows while the share count beneath it grows too, at a depressed price. Second, two dated supply events land in this window: the Series A preferred transfer restriction lapses July 31, 2026, two weeks out, alongside a 30% step-down in Allianz's common lock-up, and a Form S-3 resale shelf covering 3,053,263 Class A shares went effective around July 10, 2026. Neither is large on its own — the shelf is about 2.8% of the Class A count — but this is a thinly traded, poorly covered micro-cap with a float near 59.7 million shares, where modest supply moves price. Third, the operating base keeps burning at the reported line: the company has posted net losses every year since listing, most recently $119.7 million in 2025, and cash is $39.7 million against $77.2 million of total debt. The adjusted EBITDA that carries the story does not survive to the bottom line. Fourth, the franchise itself leaked assets — net client outflows of $0.2 billion in the first quarter of 2026 — and management churn compounds the risk: the co-founder chief executive was ousted March 30, 2026, the international president departed, an interim chief executive is in the seat, and a new chief financial officer took over July 1, 2026. In a relationship business, departing principals and departing assets tend to travel together. The specific event that would decimate the stock in this window is the quietest one: the special committee simply going dark, or disclosing that the review concluded without a transaction. Given the disclosed absence of any timeline, there is no date by which that risk resolves.
positioning_washout: The shareholder base is concentrated and structurally awkward, but the mechanical selling here runs the wrong direction for the thesis. Allianz holds about 26% of the Class A stock (subject to a 24.9% ownership cap that pushes excess into non-voting Class C shares), Constellation holds preferred and common, and ousted co-founder Michael Tiedemann holds 9.8% — leaving a small, thinly traded public float of roughly 59.7 million shares with poor sell-side coverage. Our watch board tagged this a forced-seller flow on the theory that overhang clears and the price recovers. That mechanic does not survive verification. The verified supply is the Form S-3 that went effective around July 10, 2026, registering 3,053,263 Class A shares — about 2.8% of the 110.7 million Class A outstanding — for holders who took stock as consideration in the April 2023 Alvarium Wealth Management acquisition. That is acquisition earn-out housekeeping, not a distressed forced seller, and it adds supply rather than removing it. The July 31, 2026 lapse of the Series A preferred transfer restriction, and the concurrent 30% step-down in Allianz's staged common lock-up, are likewise permissions to sell, not clearing events. Critically, the largest holder is not a forced seller at all: Allianz reads as a would-be acquirer, is bound by a standstill through July 31, 2027, has a staged lock-up on its common running to July 31, 2027, and is accumulating rather than distributing — it took 1,272,328 shares as payment-in-kind dividends on July 2, 2026. So there is no washout to buy. The genuine mechanical pressure is the opposite one: the preferred pays part of itself in new common each period, a steady, price-insensitive issuance into a thin float. A capitulation flush toward the low-$2s on that dilution and the mid-2026 supply is plausible, but it would be the start of price discovery toward the residual's true worth, not a bottom to be bought.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now. AlTi Global is a legitimate special situation -- a real, sticky franchise with $90.1 billion under advisement, 96% client retention, an improving margin, three activist filers and a J.P. Morgan mandate -- and it still fails both tests that would earn capital in this funnel.

The catalyst is soft and undated, and it is now decaying. The December 9, 2025 announcement said in terms that there is no definitive timeline; eleven months after J.P. Morgan was retained there is no buyer, no price, no drop-dead date and no vote. But the decisive evidence is what the company said itself. Asked on the May 11, 2026 call when review expenses would normalize, interim chief executive Nancy Curtin answered that AlTi is “evaluating opportunities that come as opposed to a strategic review process in place at the moment.” The formal sale process is not running. Her chief financial officer corroborated it on cost grounds -- the advisory fees “should start to diminish back half of the year” -- and advisory fees are the truest instrument for measuring whether a banker is still working. Two further markers point the same way: the June 17, 2026 annual meeting, the natural forcing window, passed with a routine slate and no contest; and the June 25, 2026 chief financial officer succession was framed as “a long-planned internal leadership transition designed to support AlTi’s next phase of growth” -- standalone language, not deal language. The arc runs from “we are for sale” to “nothing to report” to normal-course succession.

The deeper finding is why it stalled, and it is not a haggle that patience resolves. The preferred stack is the thesis. Roughly $352 million of Allianz Series A and Constellation Series C preferred -- $290 million of face accreted, each compounding at 9.75% -- sits ahead of a $531 million common, so the enterprise is capitalized near $921 million against about $58 to $60 million of normalized adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization), roughly 15 times, for an asset class that transacts at 9 to 13. Run a buyer’s real multiple and the common is left at about $2.10 to $2.65 -- below today’s $3.58. The bidders are not lowballing. Press reporting quotes a mathematical disparity between what a sponsor would pay on a reasonable multiple of AlTi’s cash flow and its market cap and enterprise value: read plainly, the buyers think the stock is already above their pay-line. The special committee is holding out for a number the arithmetic does not produce. The one structure that clears is Allianz rolling its own preferred and buying the rest -- but that makes the buyer a conflicted insider who holds the instrument capping everyone else’s value, with no disclosed majority-of-the-minority protection. The best-positioned bidder is the one most motivated to pay least.

That reframes our own board’s entry. The forced-seller flow that put this name on the list does not exist as described. What I could verify is a 3,053,263-share resale shelf effective around July 10, 2026 -- 2.8% of the Class A count, from 2023 Alvarium acquisition holders -- and a July 31, 2026 lapse of the preferred transfer restriction alongside a 30% step-down in Allianz’s common lock-up. Both are supply. The largest holder is a would-be acquirer under a standstill, not a seller, and it is accumulating through payment-in-kind dividends -- it took 1,272,328 shares on July 2, 2026. There is no overhang clearing and no washout to buy; the one hard date in the file has the opposite sign to the thesis it was filed under.

Nor is there a floor. Tangible common equity is roughly negative $550 million once $815.9 million of goodwill and intangibles comes out -- about 72% of the balance sheet is acquisition accounting. The company has never posted a reported profit: losses of $165.6 million, $103.0 million and $119.7 million in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Cash is $39.7 million against $77.2 million of debt. Nothing tangible, contractual or earnings-based stops the price. The $2.75 low is a chart reference, not a backstop.

So the asymmetry inverts: about +23% to a generous 16-times take-out at $4.40, against about -35% to $2.30 if the process lapses, with the likelier path being the bad one. And time is the adversary rather than the ally -- the rarest failure mode in this funnel. The preferred compounds at 9.75%, roughly $34 million a year or $0.23 a share, and settles part of itself in newly issued stock at multi-year-low prices, so every quarter of delay grows both the claim ahead of the common and the share count beneath it. A special situation is supposed to pay you for waiting as a dated catalyst approaches. This one charges you.

This is not a case for waiting on a flush either, which is why it is a pass rather than a watchlist item: a cheaper price would not fix a structure in which the equity sits behind a growing preferred with no floor. The honest trigger to revisit is narrow and knowable -- a signed agreement with disclosed terms that clears the $352 million preferred with room to spare. Underwrite that on the terms if it ever prints. Do not own the hope.

The bidders have said so almost in terms. Press reporting quotes "a mathematical disparity between what a private equity sponsor would pay for a reasonable multiple on AlTi's cash flow and its market cap and enterprise value." Translated: **the buyers think the stock is already too expensive.** When the bidders' complaint is that the tape is above their pay-line, the sale is not a source of upside — it is a source of downward price discovery.

The one structure that clears is Allianz rolling its Series A rather than cashing it, and buying the common it does not own. That is real. But note who it makes the buyer: a conflicted insider holding the instrument that caps everyone else's value, with no disclosed majority-of-the-minority protection. The best-positioned bidder is the one most motivated to pay least.

## 4. Claims versus financials

| Management claim (Q1 2026) | The evidence |
|---|---|
| "$73 million in total revenue, representing 28% growth" | True, but **$21M was lumpy investment distributions, up 75%** — of which ~$18M came from a single manager, Zebedee, on its 15.3% 2025 return. Recurring fees grew 16%. The headline overstates the run-rate. |
| "Adjusted EBITDA... $15 million, up 21%" | True, up 32% sequentially — but driven by the same incentive income plus the absence of a prior-quarter bonus. Not durable. |
| "costs remain too high and addressing that is a near-term priority" | Credible and corroborated: reported operating expenses **rose** $18M year-over-year to $84M; normalized expenses $58M versus $45M. Management is candid the numbers are bad. |
| "anchored in high recurring revenues and long-duration client relationships" | Fair. $52M of recurring fees is the majority of revenue; 830+ ultra-wealthy families at ~$60M average; **96% retention since 2021**. The franchise is authentic. |
| FY2025: revenue $255M (+25%), adjusted EBITDA $35M (+45%) | Alongside an **operating loss of $74M and a net loss near $120M**. Adjusted EBITDA and reality are far apart here. |

Balance sheet: **goodwill of $384.6M plus intangibles of $431.3M is $815.9M against $1,138M of total assets** — about 72% is acquisition accounting, the residue of an expensive 2023 blank-cheque roll-up. Retained earnings are negative $410.3M.

Credit where due: management's account of the *business* is broadly honest, and Curtin did not oversell the review. Candor is not the problem. The arithmetic is.

## 5. The floor — this is the weakest link

This funnel exists to buy defined-risk asymmetry: a hard-dated catalyst above a verified floor. Test the floor honestly. What backstops $3.58?

- **A deal-break price?** There is no deal. Nothing to break.
- **Cash?** $39.7M against $77.2M of debt. Net debt, not net cash.
- **Liquidation or recovery value?** The common sits behind $352M of accreting preferred. In a liquidation it is a stub, plausibly zero.
- **Tangible book?** Roughly **negative $550M** once $815.9M of goodwill and intangibles comes out.
- **Earnings?** Never profitable on a reported basis: net losses of $165.6M (2023), $103.0M (2024), $119.7M (2025).
- **The tape?** The 52-week low is $2.75; the 200-day average is $3.92. Grinding down, not basing.

The honest no-deal value is **$2.10–$2.65** on sponsor math, with a genuine clearing print lower still. The practical adverse case is a break of the $2.75 low toward **~$2.30**. None of that is a floor in the sense this funnel requires. It is a forecast of where a subordinated stub settles — no contract, no cash, no acquirer underwriting it. **The "floor" is an estimate, not a backstop.**

## 6. The dated events cut the wrong way

The verifiable hard dates all add supply rather than forcing value out:

- **31 July 2026** (two weeks out): the transfer restriction on the Series A preferred lapses, and a further 30% of Allianz's common becomes transferable under its staged lock-up (full release 31 July 2027).
- **~10 July 2026**: the S-3 resale shelf went effective — 3,053,263 Class A shares, ~2.8% of the Class A count.

Both are permissions to sell. Neither is a clearing event. **The single hard date in the file has the opposite sign to the thesis it was filed under.**

Meanwhile the payment-in-kind dividend is a *reverse* forcing function: it compounds the claim ahead of the common at 9.75% and settles part of itself in new stock at multi-year-low prices, into a thin ~59.7 million share float with poor coverage.

## 7. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- Management stated on 11 May 2026 there is no review process in place "at the moment" — only reactive evaluation of inbound proposals. **The company has verbally downgraded its own catalyst.**
- Eleven months with J.P. Morgan and no bid; Corient walked; a reported impasse on a $600M+ gap that the arithmetic says cannot close.
- Buyers say the stock is *already* above their pay-line.
- $352M of preferred compounding at 9.75% ahead of a $531M common, settling part of itself in new shares. Time is a cost to the common, not an option premium.
- The most credible bidder (Allianz) is a conflicted insider with no disclosed minority protection.
- Tangible common equity ~negative $550M; never profitable on a reported basis; cash $39.7M.
- Governance rupture: founder-CEO ousted 30 March 2026 and now filing 13Ds against the company he built; international president departed; new CFO from 1 July 2026. Companies rarely change all three while closing a sale.
- **Net client outflows of $0.2 billion in Q1 2026** — the franchise leaked assets in the quarter the story was strongest. In a relationship business, departing principals and departing assets travel together.
- The 17 June annual meeting passed uncontested; the CFO succession was framed around "the next phase of growth."

**Green flags**

- The operating business is genuinely improving: revenue +28%, adjusted EBITDA +21% to $14.9M, margin 20% versus 13%, $20M of savings targeted by year-end, normalized expenses down $19M sequentially on zero-based budgeting.
- The franchise is real and sticky: $90.1B under advisement, $48.7B under management (+9%), 830+ relationships, 96% retention — a narrow but authentic switching-cost moat.
- Q1 2026 GAAP net income from continuing operations was positive at $8M.
- Three motivated 13D filers and a J.P. Morgan mandate: the option is live, even if poorly priced.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING.** Not the operating business, which is slowly improving — the *event*. Every dated marker since March 2026 has moved against the catalyst: the process wound down to reactive posture, the annual meeting passed uncontested, the advisory fees are being guided off, the CFO succession was framed for a standalone future, and the preferred accreted another $6.25M. (The prior pass read this as PIVOTING on the leadership change; the new evidence in section 2 makes DETERIORATING the more accurate read of the event we are actually underwriting.)

**The one thing the director must weigh: the spread runs the wrong way.** This funnel buys a live price *below* an event-resolved value. Here the $3.58 price sits **above** what any disclosed bidder can rationally pay — sponsors clear at $2.10–$2.65 after the preferred, and even a generous strategic take-out at a full 16x lands near $4.40, about +23%. Against roughly −35% to a low retest on the likelier no-deal path, the asymmetry inverts. There is no defined risk here because there is no floor — only a subordinated stub behind $352M of paper that accretes whether or not anyone ever bids.

And time is the adversary rather than the ally — the rarest failure mode in this funnel. A special situation is supposed to pay you for waiting as a dated catalyst approaches. This one charges you about $0.23 a share a year.

On moat and secular risk, which are secondary in an event name: ultra-wealthy wealth management carries a narrow but real moat built on relationship intangibles and switching costs, evidenced by 96% retention — but the continuing net outflows and the governance rupture mark it as eroding at the margin. There is no terminal secular threat to independent wealth management itself; fee compression bites hardest at the mass-affluent end, and artificial intelligence reads as a tool for these advisers rather than a replacement (AlTi is deploying it as such). The terminal value is not melting. That is not the problem. The problem is that the common's claim on it is deeply subordinated and shrinking every quarter.
